title: IREN Clears Its Pivot to AI as Milestone Delays Reveal the Bill
subtitle: Sequential revenue surged and margins hit 86%, but execution risks and debt now dominate the equity story.
summary: IREN generated 88% of its revenue from AI cloud infrastructure last quarter as it wound down legacy bitcoin mining operations. A rescheduled delivery timeline with anchor tenant Microsoft leaves the company racing to fund billions in capital commitments without diluting equity.

bodyHtml:
After tech took its sharpest single-day beating in years, shares of IREN were up roughly 19% in morning trading. The rebound outpaced the broader semiconductor bounce. Investors finally got a clean look at the company's complete reinvention.

Strip away the market noise, and the core operation is straightforward. Think of IREN as the landlord who owns both the apartment building and the power plant down the block. The company controls the three rarest ingredients in AI: cheap land, proprietary grid connections, and custom liquid-cooled data center shells. It rents that infrastructure out to AI developers and hyperscalers on multi-year contracts.

That business model places IREN right at the critical bottleneck of the AI boom. Tech giants are starved for electrical capacity, and securing new grid access can take half a decade. IREN already holds roughly five gigawatts of secured power across four countries. Instead of waiting years for utility permits, clients plug directly into operational power.

This quarter marked the moment the old company died. AI Cloud brought in $200 million, surging 182% sequentially and capturing 88% of total revenue. Bitcoin mining, the company's original cash cow, shrank to $28 million and will be essentially phased out by year-end. Yet year-over-year revenue actually fell 5% to $228 million. The company is actively shrinking legacy operations faster than its new GPU clusters can turn on.

The demand side looks almost insatiable. Revenue backlog jumped to $20.3 billion, with roughly two-thirds tied to investment-grade counterparties, Microsoft chief among them. Recent contract pricing even topped $40 million per megawatt for short-term deals. Customers are so eager for capacity that some are prepaying 90% of their GPU hardware costs upfront just to secure space.

Yet the celebration met an immediate reality check on the delivery schedule. Chief executive Daniel Roberts pushed the company's target for commissioning over $4 billion in contracted annual recurring revenue from year-end into January or February. The anchor tenant behind that move is Microsoft, which requested upgrades to the network infrastructure across its Texas deployments to support newer frontier models. The contract protects IREN from financial penalties caused by client changes, but commercial details are still being hammered out.

A short seller would argue that IREN is behaving more like an overstretched construction crew than a pristine utility. Bloomberg reported on Nov. 5 that Microsoft is souring on neocloud providers over project delays and spiraling costs, specifically reviewing cabling snags at IREN's Texas site. Microsoft's leadership has pointed to third-party data center bottlenecks on three straight calls. If hyper-scaler spending cools, those eye-popping contract backlogs become heavy delivery liabilities rather than guaranteed windfalls. What proves the bears right is another delayed commissioning date, contract renegotiations that hand Microsoft fee credits, or any move to patch funding gaps through equity dilution.

That balance sheet gap is the real elephant in the room. Net debt skyrocketed from $216 million to $4.43 billion in three months as the company funded massive hardware purchases. IREN still faces $15 billion of remaining planned capital expenditures for fiscal 2027. While cash and committed GPU financing cover $9 billion, the remaining $6 billion depends entirely on favorable capital market conditions.

Here is what has to happen for the stock to re-rate from levels still more than 70% below last year's high. AI Cloud gross margin is already exceptional at 86%, meaning unit profitability is not the issue. Wall Street is discounting the shares because it views IREN as an indebted builder hostage to a single giant customer. To unlock a higher valuation multiple, IREN must turn on its January deployments on time, finalize commercial terms with Microsoft without granting discounts, and lock down that $6 billion of financing without diluting shareholders.

What we are watching is the commissioning of its next Childress capacity in January. If those liquid-cooled racks go live on schedule, IREN proves it can run with the biggest names in cloud computing. If suppliers or cabling drag the timeline further into 2027, the market will price the company strictly by its debt load.
